subject: ANTH
additional_information: This course is fully online. ANTH250 recommended, but not required. This undergraduate course, suitable for both majors and non-majors, will outline Neandertal biology, behavior, and current debates over the place of the Neandertals in human evolution. The main goal of the course is an up to date understanding about who the Neandertals were, and how they lived, through the examination of paleontological, archaeological, and molecular data. What did they look like? What did they eat? What sort of tools did they make? Were they our ancestors or not? What’s this I hear about a cave bear cult? As we evaluate the available evidence (and its limitations), we will also investigate the history of scientific and popular thought about Neandertals, and how it has reflected changes in broader societal attitudes over time. The course will include in-class, hands-on laboratory activities and open discussions. The reading list will range from selected journal articles to excerpts from popular literature like Clan of the Cave Bear.

subject: ANTH
course_name: BIOLOGICAL ANTHROPOLOGY: Evolution and Human Diversity
additional_information: This course will be offered fully online and blended (a mix of "real-time" and asynchronous sessions).  The story of our evolution and prevailing theories explaining how and why it proceeded are famously contentious. This three-field-oriented course (encompassing archaeological, cultural, and biological anthropological perspectives) is organized as a series of “capsules” investigating specific contemporary and historical controversies in human evolution, and using these capsules to introduce and elaborate upon basic anthropological principles. Pre-req: One of ANTH100, ANTH240, ANTH250, BIOL184 or permission of the department.

subject: ANTH
course_name: METHOD AND THEORY: Myth in Life
additional_information: This course engages students in both employing and critiquing anthropological methods and theories for analyzing “myth” and storytelling practices. Case studies consist of traditional stories from peoples across the globe paired with ethnographies. Emphasis is placed on the global diversity in how stories are performed and how meanings are embodied beyond the narrative arts.

subject: COM
course_name: ADVANCED MANAGEMENT TOPICS: Fundraising for Social Purpose Organizations & Enterprises
additional_information: Building a revenue profile is essential to accomplishing any organization’s mission – especially when you lead with social/environmental impact. In this course, students will gain perspective on how to foster meaningful collaborations and partnerships with the purpose of building a strong, sustainable revenue profile for your social purpose organization, including for-profits (eg B Corps, co-operatives) and non-profits (eg charities, community organizations). Students will develop business development skills, including how to foster meaningful sales relationships (without “selling your soul”). This course will use the revenue diversification canvas approach to run through types of revenue development, culminating with a strategic financial model that can be employed in their organization. Students will leave with a better understanding on how to strategically build financial impact models for organizations that lead with purpose.

additional_information: Topic Description: Did Ice Age hunters contribute to the extinction of woolly mammoths? Did the race to build Rapa Nui’s statues trigger ecological collapse? How did the First Peoples of the Pacific Northwest adapt to climate shifts, rising seas, and earthquakes over 13,000 years? Humans have long shaped and responded to environmental change. This course critically examines our evolving relationship with ecosystems through Historical Ecology, Environmental Archaeology, and Paleoethnobotany. While global in scope, it emphasizes western North America’s past 13,000 years of Ethnoecology, exploring how past adaptations can inform today’s challenges, from climate change to food security, fostering resilience for the future.

course_name: SPECIAL TOPICS CLINICAL PSYCH: Community Applications in Health, Education and Sport
additional_information: This course highlights clinical psychologists’ roles beyond the assessment and treatment of psychological disorders. We learn how to effectively promote mental resilience into health, school and athletic settings. Recognizing the limits of one’s competencies and expanding those competencies in deeply ethical way is emphasized. Learners will enhance their dialogue and facilitation skills through journal article discussions and interactive learning modules.

subject: PSYC
course_name: ADV SPCL TPCS:PSYC: Thinking, Fast and Slow
additional_information: Our decisions range from fast, intuitive responses to slow deliberations. These two modes of reasoning are classified as intuitive and analytical, respectively. Intuitive reasoning is fast, automatic, and effortless, while analytical reasoning is slow, contemplative, and effortful. In this course, we will explore the cognitive processes underlying each mode. For instance, intuitive reasoning involves the habitualization of decisions through reinforcement learning, whereas analytical reasoning requires the employment of effort through cognitive control. At the fulcrum of these modes lies a heated debate in cognitive science: how do we decide which mode to engage? We will also examine the competing cognitive models that seek to explain this mechanism of choice.
